headings: # Before You Try to Go Deep: the depth drafts, checked against the whole article (not in)
intro: Blue is what the article, or another draft here, already says. Cut, these drafts would carry only what's new in the guide's depth passage: turning the depth down isn't giving up on your little one, and changing the dose isn't failing; a no to the whole inner-child idea is a different thing (drop the words, don't sneak them back in, and looking after yourself goes on in your own words); going shallower, and coming back out to the room in the middle of an exercise if you can't stop and come back, instead of trying one technique after another; an eyes-open hello as the gentle way back in; a full pause as the last resort, made specific, with no peeks, and a return at or below the last level that worked; and settling how a hard session landed before stepping back up (no draft has that one yet).

The depth and pleasantness passages in the guide share four points (the stop-and-come-back test, eyes open before imagery, making it easier, coming back gradually). Said once instead: the during-a-session steps here, where the guide has them, and the after-a-session read in the pleasantness group.

rows.label: Depth draft 1
rows.text: Your little one will still be there later. Some people want out of the whole inner-child idea, though ("this just isn't me"), and that's a different thing. If that's you, I wouldn't keep sneaking it back in through some "gentler" version, or start calling the dishes reparenting. Looking after yourself and keeping yourself safe can happen in whatever words feel like yours. Same with figuring out where you're headed, and getting support from people.

headings: ## Your Body Might Need Some Love First: the pleasantness drafts, checked against the whole article (not in)
intro: Cut, these would carry what's new here: how pleasant a session was doesn't tell you whether it was too much (whether it helped is already in When to Change the Strategy); grief, fear, frustration and bad dreams are expected, hard isn't harm, and staying present isn't enough by itself; how the next few days went, whether you want to go back toward it, and whether it felt hard but workable or just too much (no draft has that last one yet); not calling it harm too fast either; one change at a time while you're finding your level, several at once if you're getting worse (shorter, less imagery, better timing, more symbolic, eyes open, more support); coming back gradually, at the edge where you can learn; and dreams and imagery as material about what matters now, not evidence, and not something to suggest or rebuild a memory from.

rows.label: Pleasantness draft 1
rows.text: Whatever you try from that map, I wouldn't go by how pleasant a session felt to tell whether it was good for you. This kind of work can bring up grief and fear, and sometimes hard dreams, or stuff you'd rather never have met. A session can also be really intense and get you nowhere. Even staying present the whole time doesn't tell you enough by itself. It's a bit like the gym, where sore and injured can feel pretty similar that evening, and it's the next few days that tell you which one it was.
rows.after: When your nervous system is flooded

source.quote: Do not use pleasantness as the only safety meter either.

rows.note: Alone 100% Human (101) in turn 34. (Your embedded map post sits between the paragraph before and this one.)

rows.label: Pleasantness draft 2
rows.text: So how were the next few days? How did you sleep, and could you get through your day okay? Do you want to go back toward what came up, or is some part of you saying no? (And could you have stopped and come back to the room, if you'd needed to? If not, I'd keep my eyes open next time, before any imagery.) If you honestly can't tell yet, I wouldn't rush to call it healing or harm. I'd just make the next one a bit easier, one change at a time, so you learn what made the difference. If you're getting worse, though, change several things at once, and have someone steady with you.

source.quote: Ask four things: could you stop and return, do you actually want to go back toward it, did it feel difficult-but-workable rather than simply too much or unwanted, and how did you recover afterward in sleep and ordinary functioning?

rows.text: Bring the challenge back gradually, and only when you want to and you're recovering well. If you're not sure yet whether you want to, you can wait. Some people try to toughen themselves up in a cauldron, but what you're looking for is the edge where you can actually learn. Those dreams and images that come up can show what feels important or frightening right now. Sometimes they show what feels missing, or what feels needed. They aren't evidence that what you saw in them happened, though, and shouldn't be used to confirm a memory or rebuild one. Or to suggest one.

headings: ### Also Look Outward: the isolation drafts and C2, after your C1 (not in)
intro: What's new here: being alone with it as part of the wound, and reaching toward people as the grown-up's care, with the word "reparenting" optional; not having to get yourself sorted first (the guide's examples besides texting: setting up the visit, asking the social worker, walking into a room where people share something real); C2's honesty points (none of them is in the article yet); other people aren't a reassurance machine, and support goes both ways (no draft has these yet); more than one place to belong, keeping the good people, not every door opening; and the Protector on groups.

rows.label: Isolation draft 1
rows.text: Maybe part of what your little one went through was being alone with it. Then reaching toward people can be part of this work too, and you can call that reparenting if you like the word. Some people figure, "I'll get myself sorted out first, and then I'll be fit company for anybody." I don't think a decent parent would ask that of a lonely kid. So sometimes the grown-up thing to do is just to text someone first.
rows.after: Then there are people you're just getting to know.

source.quote: If isolation itself is part of the wound, reaching toward people may be one way the adult side provides care.

rows.label: Honesty draft (C2)
rows.text: And reaching out doesn't mean telling strangers everything. Privacy isn't fakery. People can earn more of you by how they handle the smaller things you tell them, and how they take it when you say no. But if a relationship is getting deep and you're still keeping up a fake normal, happy version of yourself to hold onto it, I'd either bring more of the truth in, carefully, or let it be less deep for now. (If telling could put you in real danger, like violence, or being outed where that isn't safe, protect yourself first.) And when someone finally accepts you, it can feel amazing. It still doesn't prove you're meant for each other, or that they've earned your trust yet.
